(Section)

Having understood this, *al-waswās* (the whisperer) is on the pattern *fi'lāl* (فعلال) derived from *waswasa* (وسوس).

The root meaning of *al-waswasa* (whispering) is a movement or a hidden sound that is not perceived, so one is wary of it.

Thus *al-waswās* is a hidden insinuation into the soul, either by a faint sound that is heard only by the one it is addressed to, or without any sound, as the Shaytan whispers (*yusawisu*) to the servant.

From this is the *waswasat al-hulī* (the jingling of an ornament), which is its hidden movement in the ear.

The apparent meaning, and God knows best, is that it was called *waswasa* because of its closeness and its close proximity to the place of whispering from the devils of mankind, which is the ear. So it is called *waswasat al-hulī*, because it is a sound adjacent to the ear, like the whispered speech that the Shaytan casts into the ear of the one he whispers to.

Since *al-waswasa* is speech that the whisperer repeats and emphasises to the one he casts it upon, they repeated its wording to correspond to the repetition of its meaning. So they said *waswasa, waswasatan*. They took into account the repetition of the wording so that the repetition of its referent would be understood from it.

A parallel to this is what preceded regarding their making the movement of the wording correspond to the movement of its meaning, such as *al-dawarān* (turning), *al-ghalayān* (boiling), *al-nazawān* (leaping), and their kind.

A parallel to this is *zalzala, dakdaka, qalqala*, and *kabkaba al-shay'* (to overturn a thing). This is because *al-zalzala* is a repeated movement; likewise *al-dakdaka* and *al-qalqala*. Likewise *kabkaba al-shay'*: when he overturns it in a distant place, so it is overturned in it, *kabban ba'da kabbin* (again and again), as in His saying, ﴿So they will be thrown headlong into it, they and the deviators﴾.

Similar to this is *radradahu*, when he repeats a crushing blow, one after another.

Similar to this is *dharradhara*, when he scatters a thing bit by bit. Similar to this is *sarsara al-bāb* (the door creaked), when its creaking is repeated.

Similar to this is *mataṭa al-kalām* (he drawled out the speech), when he draws it out piece by piece. Similar to this is *kafkafa al-shay'*, when he repeatedly gathers it in, and this is abundant.

It is known from this that whoever makes this quadriliteral (*rubā'ī*) equivalent in meaning to the doubled triliteral has erred. This is because the triliteral does not indicate repetition, unlike the repeated quadriliteral. So when you say *dharra al-shay'*, *ṣarra al-bāb*, *kaffa al-thawb*, or *radda al-ḥabb*, it does not indicate repetition of the action, unlike *dhardhara, ṣarṣara, radrada*, and the like.

So reflect on it, for it conforms to the Arabic rule of making the wording follow the meanings.

This has already been pointed out, so there is no need to repeat it.

Likewise their saying *ajja al-'ijl* (the calf lowed) when it makes a sound. If its sound is repeated, they say *'ajja'ja*. Likewise *thajja al-mā'* (the water poured) when it is poured; if this is repeated it is said *thajthaja*.

The point is that since the whisperer repeats his whispering and continues it, it is called *waswas*.

(Section)

Having understood this, the grammarians differed concerning the word *al-waswās*: is it an adjective (*waṣf*) or a verbal noun (*maṣdar*)? There are two opinions.

We will mention the argument of each opinion, then clarify the correct one of the two, by God's help and grace.

As for those who held that it is a verbal noun, they argued that its verb is of the pattern *fa'lala*, and the active participle of *fa'lala* is only *mufa'lil*, as in *mudaḥraj, musarhif, mubayṭir,* and *musayṭir*. Likewise it is from the pattern *fa'ala* of the form *mif'al*, as in *miqṭa'*, *mukhraj*, and its kind. So if *al-waswās* were an adjective it would be said *mūsawis*. Do you not see that the active participle of *zalzala* is *muzalzil*, not *zalzāl*? Likewise from *dakdaka* is *mudakdik*, and this is regular. This shows that *al-waswās* is a verbal noun used as an attribute in an intensive sense, or it is on the elision of a modified noun, its estimated form being *dhū al-waswās* (the possessor of whispering).

They said: the evidence for this is also the poet's verse:

*Tasma'u lil-ḥulā bihā waswāsā*
(You hear the jingling of ornaments therein, a whispering.)

So this is a verbal noun with the meaning of *al-waswasa*, the same.

Those of the other opinion said: the proof that it is an adjective is that *fa'lala* has two types.

One is sound and has no repetition in it, such as *daḥraja, sarhaf,* and *bayṭar*. The analogous verbal noun of this verb is *fa'lala* (*fa'lalah*), such as *al-daḥraja, al-sarhafa*, and *al-bayṭara*, and the form *fi'lān* with a kasra on the first letter, such as *al-sarhāf* and *al-daḥrāj*. Its active participle is *mufa'lil*, such as *mudaḥraj* and *mubayṭir*.

The second is the doubled triliteral *fa''ala*, such as *zalzala, dakdaka*, and *waswasa*. This is a branch of the bare *fa'lala* that is free of repetition, because the original state is freedom from repetition. The verbal noun of this type and its active participle are equivalent to the verbal noun and participle of the first. So its verbal noun comes on the form *fa'lala*, such as *al-waswasa* and *al-zalzala*, and the form *fi'lāl*, such as *al-zilzāl*.

The more analogous of the two verbal nouns, and the more suited to the two types of *fa'lala*, is the *fi'lāl* form, for two reasons.

The first: *fa'lala* resembles *af'ala* in number of letters, in the vowelling of the first, third and fourth letters being fatḥa, and the second being sukūn. So they made *if'āl* the verbal noun of *af'ala*, and *fi'lāl* the verbal noun of *fa'lala*, so that the two verbal nouns would correspond as the two verbs correspond. Thus *fi'lāl* was more deserving of this pattern than *fa'lala*.

The second: the basic rule is that the verbal noun's pattern differs from the pattern of its verb, and the difference of *fi'lāl* from *fa'lala* is greater than the difference of *fa'lala* from it. So *fi'lāl* was more entitled to the verbal noun than *fa'lala*, or they were equal in regularity, although *fa'lala* is more preponderant and more common in usage. This is the basic rule.

They have indeed brought a verbal noun of this repeated pattern with an open first letter.

They said: *waswasa al-shayṭānu waswāsan*, and *wa'wa'a al-kalb wa'wā'an* when the dog barked, and *'azʿaza al-sahm 'azʿāṭan*. The regular form that follows analogy is *fi'lāl* with a kasra on the first letter, or *fa'lala*. This open form is rare. This is because the sound quadriliteral is the root of the repeated one, and the verbal noun of the sound one, despite being the root, has come only as *fa'lala* and *fi'lāl* with kasra. So it was not fitting for the repeated quadriliteral, being a branch, to have its verbal noun other than this. Because the branch does not contradict its root, but follows its pattern. This requires that its verbal noun not be on *fa'lāl* with fatḥa. If it is anomalous, it is memorised and not extended beyond it.

They said: moreover, *fi'lāl* with an open first letter has become frequent as an adjective derived from the repeated *fa'lala*, so that there would be a parallel to *fa'āl* of the triliteral, because they share the same pattern. This requires that *fa'lāl* have no share in verbal nouns, just as *fa'āl* has no share in them. So for this reason they considered *waswās*, *wa'wā'*, and *'azʿāẓ* as verbal nouns to be rare. Their proper function is to be attributes indicating intensity for the verbs' masdars.

They said: and once this is established, the proper ruling for what occurs among them that is ambiguous between verbal noun and adjective is to take it as an adjective, following the more common and prevalent usage, and avoiding the anomalous.

So whoever claims that *al-waswās* is a verbal noun with *dhū* estimated before it, his statement is outside analogy and the prevalent usage.

Two things indicate the invalidity of what he held.

The first: every verbal noun to which *dhū* is estimated as a prefix is more purely a verbal noun than it is an adjective, as in *riḍā, ṣawm,* and *fiṭr*. The open *fi'lāl* has not been established as purely a verbal noun except in three words only: *waswās, wa'wā'*, and *'azʿāẓ*. Yet denying verbal-nounhood here is possible. This is because the most that can be cited as evidence for verbal-nounhood is their saying *waswasa ilayhi al-shayṭānu waswāsan*. But this is not decisively a verbal noun, because it may be intended as an adjective, with *waswāsan* in the accusative as a circumstantial state (*ḥāl*), an emphatic circumstantial state. For a circumstantial state can emphasise its verb when they agree in wording and meaning, as in His saying, ﴿And We sent you to mankind as a messenger﴾ and ﴿He subjected for you the night and the day, the sun and the moon, and the stars are subjected by His command﴾.

Indeed, the verbal-nounhood of *al-waswās* is decisively established only if one hears: *a'ūdhu billāhi min waswās al-shayṭān* (I seek refuge in God from the whispering of the Shaytan) and similar expressions in which *waswās* is attached to its agent, as was heard for *waswasa*. But where is that for you? Bring its witness. Thus it is decisively established that *waswās* is a verbal noun, not in the sense of being in the accusative after the verb.

The second argument refuting the claim that *waswāsan* is a verbal noun with *dhū* estimated: a verbal noun to which *dhū* is estimated is not made feminine, dual, or plural, but keeps one form, to show its originality as a verbal noun and that the adjectival sense is incidental. So it is said: *imra'a ṣawm* (a fasting woman), *imra'atān ṣawm*, and *nisā' ṣawm*, because the meaning is *dhāt ṣawm* (a possessor of fasting), *dhātā ṣawm*, and *dhawāt ṣawm*. But the *fi'lāl* adjective is not like this; rather it is dualised, pluralised, and feminised. So we say: *rajul tharthār* (a chatterer man), *imra'a tharthāra* (a chatterer woman), and *rijāl tharthārūn* (chatterer men). In a hadith: "The most hateful of you to me are the *tharthārūn* and the *mutafayhiqūn*." They said: *rīḥ raqrāqa* (a wind that shakes the trees), *rīḥ sasāfa* (a wind that sifts dust), and *dir' faḍfāḍa* (a loose wide coat). The verb of all of these is *fa'lala*, and the verbal noun is *fa'lala* and *fi'lāl* with kasra. Nothing in any of this has been transmitted as *fa'lāl* with fatḥa. Likewise they said: *tamtām* and *fa'fā'* (a stammerer), *liḍlāḍ* (one skilled in indicating), *fajfāj* (one who talks much), *harhār* (one who laughs), *kahkāh*, *waṭwāṭ* (a weak one), *ḥashḥāsh*, and *'asʿās* (light). It is abundant. Its verbal noun is all *fa'lala*, and the adjective is *fa'lāl* with fatḥa. Similar to it is *hafhāf* (slender), similar to it *daḥdāḥ* (short), similar to it *bajbāj* (large in body), and *tukhtākh* (one who speaks with a lisp), and *shamshām* (quick), and *shay' khashkhāsh* (a thing that makes a sound), and *qa'qā'* like it, and *asad qaḍqāḍ* (a breaking lion), and *ḥayya naḍnāḍ* (a snake that moves its tongue).

So you have seen *fa'lāl* in all of these as an adjective, not a verbal noun. What then is the matter with *al-waswās* that it is taken out of its counterparts and the analogy of its class?

Thus it is established that *waswās* is an adjective, not a verbal noun, like *tharthār, tamtām, daḥdāḥ*, and its kind.

Another aspect also indicates it: that it is described by something that cannot possibly be a verbal noun, but is decisively an adjective, namely *al-khannās*. So *al-waswās* and *al-khannās* are two attributes of a deleted modified noun, which is the Shaytan.

The omission of the modified noun is made good here by the predominance of the attribute, until it becomes like a proper name for him.

The omission of the modified noun is objectionable only when the attribute is shared, so that ambiguity arises, as with *al-ṭawīl* (tall) and *al-qabīḥ* (ugly), *al-ḥasan* (good), and the like. Then mentioning the modified noun is necessary, so that it is known that the attribute belongs to it and not to something else.

But when the attribute predominates and is exclusive, and no sharing arises in it, it functions as a noun, and omitting the modified noun is good, as with *al-muslim* (the Muslim) and *al-kāfir* (the disbeliever), *al-barr* (the righteous) and *al-fājir* (the wicked), *al-qāṣī* (the distant) and *al-dānī* (the near), *al-shāhid* (the witness) and *al-wālī* (the ruler), and the like. So omitting the modified noun here is better than mentioning it.

This distinction is preferable to the absolute position of those who prohibited omitting the modified noun without distinction.

Another thing that indicates that *al-waswās* is an adjective, not a verbal noun, is that the adjectival sense is more predominant in *fi'lāl* than the verbal-nounhood, as has been stated. So if the verbal noun were intended, *dhū* would have been prefixed to it, to remove the ambiguity and make the verbal-nounhood certain. For when a word admits both meanings equally, a clue must indicate which of them is intended. How then when the adjectival sense predominates over the verbal-nounhood?

This is unlike *ṣawm* and *fiṭr* and their kind, for they are verbal nouns that are not confused with adjectives.

When they function as adjectives, it is known that they are on an elided modified noun, or that the verbal noun is treated as an adjective for intensity, according to the two approaches on this matter.

So it is established that *al-waswās* is the Shaytan himself, and that he is a person, not a verbal noun. And God knows best.

(Section)

As for *al-khannās*: it is *fa''āl*, from *khanasa yakhnusu*, when one hides and conceals himself.

From it is the saying of Abu Hurayrah: "The Prophet (ﷺ) met me on one of the roads of Madinah while I was in a state of major impurity, so I slipped away from him."

The real meaning of the word is hiding after appearing. So it is not merely for hiding. For this reason the stars were described with it in His saying, {81:15} ﴿So I swear by the stars that recede﴾. Qatadah said: they are the stars that appear at night and recede by day, so they are hidden and not seen. Likewise 'Ali (may God be pleased with him) said: they are the stars that recede by day so they are not seen.

A group said: *al-khunnas* are the ones that return, that return every night to the direction of the east, and they are the seven wandering planets.

They said: the root of *al-khunūs* is returning backward. And *al-khannās* is derived from these two meanings. So it comes from hiding, returning, and withdrawing. For when the servant is heedless of the remembrance of God, the Shaytan squats on his heart and spreads over it, and sows in it kinds of whisperings, which are the root of all sins. When the servant remembers his Lord and seeks refuge in Him, he recedes and contracts, as a thing recedes in order to hide. That receding and contracting is also a gathering and returning, and a withdrawal from the heart outward. So it is a withdrawal and return accompanied by concealment.

*Khanasa* and *inkhanasa* indicate both meanings together. Qatadah said: *al-khannās* has a snout like the snout of a dog in the chest of a human. When the servant remembers his Lord, it recedes him.

It is said: its head is like the head of a snake. It places its head on the core of the heart, wishing for it and speaking to it. When God is remembered, it recedes. When He is not remembered, it returns and places its head, whispering to it and desiring for it.

From this verb has come the form *fa''āl*, which is intensive, rather than *khāni's* and *munkhanis*, to indicate the intensity of its fleeing and return, and the greatness of its aversion at the remembrance of God, and that this is its habit and constant practice, not that the remembrance of God occurs to it only occasionally. Rather, when God is remembered it flees, recedes, and withdraws. The remembrance of God is its goad with which it is driven off, just as a corrupter and an evildoer is driven off with goads that repel him, such as whips, iron, staves, and the like. So the remembrance of God subdues the Shaytan, pains him, and hurts him, like the whips and goads that hurt those who are struck with them.

For this reason the Shaytan of the believer is emaciated, slight, and worn out, by what the believer torments and subdues him with, namely the remembrance of God and obedience to Him.

It is reported from some of the early Muslims: the believer wears out his Shaytan as a man wears out his camel on a journey. For whenever it confronts him, he pours upon it the whips of remembrance, turning to God, seeking forgiveness, and obedience. So his Shaytan is in severe torment with him, not in the position of the Shaytan of the wicked, who is with him in ease and comfort. For this reason the latter is strong, insolent, and fierce.

Whoever does not torment his Shaytan in this world with the remembrance of God Most High, His unification, His forgiveness, and His obedience, will be tormented by his Shaytan in the Hereafter with the torment of the Fire. So everyone must either torment his Shaytan or be tormented by his Shaytan.

Reflect on how the form *al-waswās* came repeated, corresponding to his repeating a single whispering many times, until the servant becomes resolved upon it. And the form *al-khannās* came on the pattern *fa''āl*, which indicates the repetition of a kind of action. For whenever God is remembered it recedes, and then when the servant becomes heedless it returns with whispering. So the form of the two words corresponds to their two meanings.

[Section: On what the one afflicted with waswās should say and do, and what he should seek help with against whispering]

Ṣāliḥ ibn Kaysān narrated, from 'Ubayd Allāh ibn 'Abd Allāh ibn 'Utbah ibn Mas'ūd, from Ibn Mas'ūd, raising it (to the Prophet ﷺ): "The angel assigned to the heart of the son of Adam has an inspiration, and the Shaytan has an inspiration. The inspiration of the angel is a promise of good, an affirmation of the truth, and hope in its good reward. The inspiration of the Shaytan is a promise of evil, a denial of the truth, and despair of good. So when you find the inspiration of the angel, praise God and ask Him for His bounty. And when you find the inspiration of the Shaytan, seek refuge in God and ask Him for forgiveness."

"'Uthmān ibn Abi al-'Āṣ said to him: 'O Messenger of God, the Shaytan has come between me and my prayer and my recitation.' He said: 'That is a shaytan called Khinzab. When you sense him, seek refuge in God from him, and spit three times to your left.'"

"The Companions complained to him that one of them finds in himself something, alluding to a matter, and that he would rather be a piece of charcoal than speak of it. So he said: 'God is greatest, God is greatest. Praise belongs to God who has returned his scheme to whispering.'"

"He directed one who was afflicted with some of the whisperings of an infinite regress regarding the agents, when it is said to him, 'This is God who created creation; who created God?', to recite: ﴿He is the First and the Last, the Outward and the Inward, and He is Knower of all things﴾ [al-Ḥadīd: 3]."

Likewise "Ibn 'Abbās said to Abū Zumayl Simāk ibn al-Walīd al-Ḥanafī, who had asked him: 'What is something I find in my chest?' He said: 'What is it?' He said: 'I said: By God, I will not speak of it.' He said to me: 'Is it something of doubt?' I said: 'Yes.' He said to me: 'No one escapes from that, until God Mighty and Majestic revealed: ﴿So if you are in doubt about what We have sent down to you, ask those who read the Book before you﴾ [Yūnus: 94].'" He said: "He said to me: 'When you find something in yourself, say: ﴿He is the First and the Last, the Outward and the Inward, and He is Knower of all things﴾.'"

He directed them, through this verse, to the falsity of an infinite regress (tasalsul, the endless chain of causes) by the self-evident judgment of reason. The chain of created things, in its beginning, ends at a First before which there is nothing, just as in its end it ends at a Last after which there is nothing. His outwardness (zuhur) is the Highness above which there is nothing, and His inwardness (buṭūn) is the encompassing in which nothing lies beneath Him. Were there something before Him that acted upon Him, that would be the Lord, the Creator. The matter must end at a Creator who is uncreated and independent of everything else, while everything else is in need of Him, subsisting by itself, while everything subsists through Him, existing in its own essence, while everything exists through Him. He is Eternal, with no beginning. Everything other than Him, its existence after its non-existence, subsists by its own essence, while the subsistence of everything is through Him. He is the First, before whom there is nothing, and the Last, after whom there is nothing, the Outward above whom there is nothing, and the Inward beneath whom there is nothing.

The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "People will continue to ask questions until one of them says, 'This is Allah, who created the creation; but who created Allah?' Whoever finds anything of that in himself, let him seek refuge in Allah and let him desist." And He, the Exalted, has said: ﴿And if an evil prompting from Satan should afflict you, then seek refuge in Allah; indeed, He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing﴾ [Fussilat: 36].

Since Satan is of two kinds: one kind that is seen plainly, which is the devil of mankind (shayṭān al-Ins), and another kind that is not seen, which is the devil of the jinn (shayṭān al-Jinn), He, glorified and exalted, commanded His Prophet (ﷺ) that, against the evil of the devil of mankind, he should be content with turning away from them, pardoning them, and repelling with what is better; and against the evil of the devil of the jinn, with seeking refuge in Allah from him and pardoning. He combined the two kinds in Surah al-A'raf, Surah al-Mu'minun, and Surah Fussilat. Seeking refuge in recitation and remembrance is most effective in repelling the evil of the devils of the jinn, while pardon, turning away, and repelling with goodness are most effective in repelling the evil of the devils of mankind.

He said:
Nothing else is but seeking refuge, humbly,
or repelling with goodness; these two are the best of what is sought.
This is the remedy of the disease from the evil that is seen,
and that is the remedy of the disease from the evil that is hidden.

(Chapter)

His words, ﴿Who whispers in the breasts of mankind﴾, are a third attribute of the Devil.

He mentioned his whispering first, then mentioned its place second, and then mentioned that it is in the breasts of mankind third.

God has granted the Devil entry into the inside of the servant and penetration into his heart and chest. He flows through him as the blood flows. He has been assigned to the servant and does not leave him until death.

In the two Sahihs, from the hadith of al-Zuhri, from Ali ibn Husayn, from Safiyya bint Huyayy, who said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ was in seclusion (i'tikaf), so I came to visit him at night and spoke with him. Then I stood up and returned, and he stood up with me to accompany me. Her dwelling was in the house of Usama ibn Zayd. Two men of the Ansar passed by, and when they saw the Prophet ﷺ they hastened. The Prophet ﷺ said: 'Slow down, it is Safiyya bint Huyayy.' They said: 'Glory be to Allah, O Messenger of Allah!' He said: 'Indeed the Devil flows through the human being as the blood flows. I feared that he might cast into your hearts something evil,' or he said, 'something.'"

Also in the Sahih, from Abu Salama ibn Abd al-Rahman, from Abu Hurayra, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "When the call to prayer is made, the Devil turns away, breaking wind as he goes. When the call ends, he returns. When the iqama is given, he turns away again. When it ends, he returns, until he comes between a person and his heart, and says: 'Remember such-and-such, remember such-and-such,' of things he had not been remembering, until the person does not know whether he has prayed three or four. If he does not know whether he prayed three or four, let him perform the two prostrations of forgetfulness."

Among his whisperings: what is established in the Sahih from Abu Hurayra, from the Prophet ﷺ, who said: "The Devil comes to one of you and says: 'Who created such-and-such? Who created such-and-such?' until he says: 'Who created Allah?' Whoever finds that, let him seek refuge in Allah and desist."

And in the Sahih: the Companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "O Messenger of Allah, one of us finds in himself something that he would rather fall from the sky to the earth than speak of." He said: "Praise be to Allah who has turned his scheming into mere whispering."

And among his whisperings also: he occupies the heart with his talk until he makes one forget what one intends to do. For this reason forgetting is attributed to him, as one attributes a thing to its cause. The Exalted said, relating the words of the companion of Musa: ﴿Indeed I forgot the fish, and none caused me to forget it except Satan, that I should mention it﴾.

Reflect on the wisdom and majesty of the Qur'an: how it placed the seeking of refuge from the evil of the Devil, described as "the whisperer who withdraws, who whispers in the breasts of mankind," rather than saying "from the evil of his whispering," so that the seeking of refuge encompasses all of his evil. For His words, ﴿from the evil of the whisperer﴾, include all of his evil. He described him with his greatest attributes, the most severe in evil, the most powerful in effect, and the most pervasive in corruption, namely the whispering that is the beginning of intention. The heart is empty of evil and sin, so he whispers to it and the sin comes to mind; he pictures it to the soul, promises it, and makes it desired, so it becomes a craving. He adorns it and beautifies it for him, and imagines it in his imagination, until the soul inclines to it and it becomes an intention.

Then he continues to present it to him, imagine it, promise it, make it desired, and make him forget his knowledge of its harm, and conceal from him its evil outcome. He places himself between him and his contemplation, so he sees only the image of the sin and the pleasure in it, and forgets what lies beyond that. Then the intention becomes a firm resolve, and the desire for it intensifies in the heart.

Then he sends out the troops in pursuit, and the Devil sends with them reinforcements and aid. If they slacken, he stirs them up; if they falter, he drives them on.

As the Exalted said: ﴿Have you not seen that We sent the devils upon the disbelievers, inciting them with incitement?﴾ That is, driving them to sins with a driving.

Whenever they slacken or falter, the devils urge them, incite them, and stir them up. He does not cease to lead the servant to sin, and to arrange the gathering of his affairs with the subtlest trick and the most complete scheme. He has been content to take for himself the role of leader of the wicked sons of Adam, though he was the one who acted arrogantly and refused to prostrate before their father. Yet he is not satisfied with that pride and arrogance, nor is he content to become a pimp for everyone who disobeys Allah. As one of them said:

"I am amazed at Iblis in his bewilderment,
and at the ugliness of the arrogance he displayed.
He was lost before Adam over a single prostration,
and became a pimp for his offspring."

Thus the root of every sin and calamity is nothing but whispering. This is why he was described by it, so that seeking refuge from its evil would be more important than from anything else one seeks refuge from. Otherwise, his evil apart from whispering is also present.

From his evil: he is a thief who steals people's wealth. Every food or drink over which the name of Allah is not mentioned has a share for him through theft and snatching. Likewise, he spends the night in a house where the name of Allah is not mentioned, eating the food of humans without their permission, and sleeping in their houses without their command. He enters as a thief and leaves as a raider, and he points out their private faults. He commands the servant to sin, then casts into the hearts of people, awake and asleep, that he did such-and-such.

From this: the servant commits a sin that no one among the people sees, then in the morning people are talking about it. This is nothing but that the Devil adorned it for him and cast it into his heart, then whispered to the people about what he had done and cast it to them, so he made him fall into sin, then exposed him by it.

Thus the Lord, exalted is He, conceals him, while the Devil strives to uncover his concealment and disgrace him. The servant is deceived and says: "This is a sin that no one saw but Allah." He is unaware that his enemy is working to spread it and disgrace him. Few among people perceive this subtle point.

From his evil: when the servant sleeps, he ties a knot on his head that prevents him from waking.

As in the Sahih of al-Bukhari, from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, from Abu Hurayra, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "The Devil ties three knots on the back of the head of one of you when he sleeps, striking upon each knot in its place: 'The night is long, so sleep on.' If he wakes and remembers Allah, one knot is untied. If he performs wudu, another knot is untied. If he prays, all the knots are untied. Then he becomes energetic and good of spirit; otherwise he becomes evil of spirit and lazy."

From his evil: he urinates in the ear of the servant until he sleeps until morning, as established from the Prophet ﷺ: "A man was mentioned in his presence who slept the whole night until morning. He said: 'That is a man whom the Devil urinated into his ears,' or he said: 'into his ear.'" Narrated by al-Bukhari.

From his evil: he sits in wait for the son of Adam on all the paths of goodness. There is no path of goodness except that the Devil is stationed upon it, striving with all his might to prevent him from taking it. If he defies him and takes it, he hinders him in it, obstructs him, and confuses him with objections and obstacles. If he completes his deed and finishes it, he assigns to him what nullifies its effect and turns him back on his heels.

It is enough of his evil that he swore by Allah that he would surely sit in wait for the children of Adam on His straight path.

And he swore that he would surely come to them from before them, from behind them, from their right and from their left.

His evil has reached the point that he devised schemes and exerted effort in trickery until he expelled Adam from Paradise. Then that was not enough for him until he sought from his offspring a share for the Fire, from every thousand: nine hundred and ninety-nine. Then that was not enough for him until he devised a plan to nullify the call of Allah from the earth, and intended that the worship be for himself, and that he be worshipped instead of Allah. So he strives with his utmost effort to extinguish the light of Allah, nullify His call, establish the call to disbelief and polytheism, and erase monotheism and its signs from the earth.

It is enough of his evil that he confronted Ibrahim, the Friend of the Most Merciful, until his people threw him into the fire by catapult. Allah turned back his scheme against him, and made the fire coolness and peace for His friend.

He confronted the Messiah ﷺ until the Jews intended to kill him and crucify him. Allah turned back his scheme, and raised the Messiah to Himself.

He confronted Zakariyya and Yahya until they were killed.

He incited Pharaoh until he adorned for him great corruption in the earth and the claim that he was their Most High Lord.

He confronted the Prophet ﷺ and backed the disbelievers in their plot to kill him with all his might. Allah humiliates him and repels him defeated.

He sprang at the Prophet ﷺ with a flaming spark, wanting to strike him with it, while he was in prayer.

So the Prophet ﷺ said: "I curse you with the curse of Allah."

He also aided the Jews in their sorcery against the Prophet ﷺ.

If this is his condition and his aspiration in evil, how can one be freed from him except by the help of Allah, His support, and His protection?

The kinds of his evil cannot be enumerated, let alone their individual instances, since every evil in the world is caused by him. But his evil is confined to six categories. He does not cease to pursue the son of Adam until he attains one or more of them from him.

The first evil: the evil of disbelief and polytheism, and enmity toward Allah and His Messenger. When he succeeds in this from the son of Adam, he is relieved and rests from his toil with him. This is the first thing he seeks from the servant.

He does not cease until he attains it from him. When he attains that, he makes him one of his army and troops, deputizes him over his like and kind, and he becomes one of the callers and deputies of Iblis. If he despairs of him in this, and the servant is one for whom Islam was decreed in his mother's womb, he moves him to the second level of evil.

That is innovation (bid'a), and it is more beloved to him than immorality and sins, because its harm is to the religion itself, and that harm is transgressive. It is a sin from which one does not repent, it opposes the call of the messengers, and it calls to what they did not bring. It is the gateway to disbelief and polytheism.

When he attains innovation from him and makes him one of its people, he becomes his deputy and one of his callers as well.

If he defeats him at this level, and the servant is one for whom Allah has decreed the gift of the Sunnah and enmity toward the people of innovation and misguidance, he moves him to the third level of evil, which is the major sins in their various kinds. He is then most eager to make him fall into them, especially if he is a scholar who is followed. He is eager for that so that people will shun him, then he spreads his sins and transgressions among the people, and appoints from among them those who spread and publicize them, out of a supposed religiosity and nearness to Allah, while he is Iblis's deputy without knowing it. Indeed, those who love that indecency should spread among those who believe will have a painful punishment in this world and the Hereafter. This is when they love its spread and publicizing; how much more so when they themselves take charge of spreading and publicizing it, not out of sincere counsel, but out of obedience to Iblis and as his deputies. All of this is to make people shun him and shun benefiting from him.

The sins of this person, even if they reach the clouds of the sky, are less severe before Allah than the sins of those, for his are a wrong to himself, which, if he seeks forgiveness from Allah and repents to Him, Allah accepts his repentance and replaces his evil deeds with good deeds.

As for the sins of those: they are a wrong to the believers, a pursuit of their faults, and an intent to disgrace them. Allah, glory be to Him, is ever watchful; the hidden plots of the breast and the stratagems of souls are not concealed from Him.

If the Devil fails at this level, he moves him to the fourth level: the minor sins, which, when accumulated, may destroy their doer. As the Prophet ﷺ said: "Beware of belittled sins, for the likeness of them is like a people who alighted in an open desert," and he mentioned a hadith meaning that each of them brought a piece of firewood until they kindled a great fire and cooked and roasted.

He continues to make the minor sins easy for him until he makes him despise them, so that the one fearful of a major sin is in a better state than him.

If the servant defeats him at this level, he moves him to the fifth level: occupation with permissible things which have neither reward nor punishment, but whose outcome is the loss of the reward that is lost to him by occupying himself with them.

If the servant defeats him at this level, and is one who guards his time, is stingy with it, knows the measure of his breaths and their ending, and what corresponds to them of bliss and punishment, he moves him to the sixth level: that he occupies him with a lesser deed over what is better, to remove from him the excellence and deprive him of the reward of the superior deed. So he commands him to do a lesser good, urges him to it, and beautifies it for him when it entails leaving what is better and higher. Few people become aware of this. For when he sees in it a strong call and a motive toward some kind of obedience, he does not doubt that it is obedience. He hardly says: "This call is from the Devil," for the Devil does not command good. He sees that this is good, and says: "This call is from Allah."

And he is excused. His knowledge does not reach that the Devil commands seventy doors of good, either to reach through them one door of evil, or to forfeit through them a good greater than those seventy doors and more exalted and superior.

This cannot be known except by a light from Allah that He casts into the servant's heart, caused by singling out the following of the Messenger ﷺ and intense care for the ranks of deeds before Allah.

And the most beloved of them to Him, the most pleasing to Him, the most beneficial to the servant, and the most comprehensive in sincere counsel to Allah, His Messenger, His Book, and the believers, both the elite and the common folk. None knows this except one who is among the heirs of the Messenger ﷺ, his deputies in the community, and his successors on earth. Most of creation is veiled from this, so it does not occur to their hearts. And Allah bestows His favor upon whom He wills of His servants.

So when the servant defeats him in these six levels and he is exhausted, he sets upon him his party from humans and jinn with various kinds of harm, accusations of disbelief, misguidance, and innovation, and warnings against him, and seeks to bring him low and extinguish him, to disturb his heart, occupy his thought with fighting him, and prevent people from benefiting from him.

His effort continues to set upon him the people of falsehood from the devils of humans and jinn, not slackening nor faltering. Then the believer must put on the armor of war, and not take it off until death. Whenever he takes it off, he is captured or wounded, and he remains in struggle until he meets Allah.

So reflect on this section, consider its place and its great benefit, and make it your measure by which you weigh people and weigh deeds. For it will inform you of the realities of existence and the ranks of creation. And Allah is the One sought for help, and upon Him is reliance.

Had this commentary contained nothing but this section, it would have been beneficial to whoever contemplates and understands it.

(Chapter)

Reflect on the secret in His words, ﴿who whispers in the breasts of mankind﴾, and not "in their hearts." The breast is the courtyard and house of the heart. Through it incoming thoughts enter, gathering in the breast before entering the heart. It is like a vestibule to it. From the heart, commands and intentions go out to the breast, then spread among the troops. Whoever understands this understands His words: ﴿And that Allah may test what is in your breasts and purify what is in your hearts﴾.

So the Devil enters the courtyard and house of the heart, and casts into it what he wants to cast, so he whispers in the breast, and his whispering reaches the heart. This is why the Exalted said: ﴿So Satan whispered to him﴾, and did not say "in him," because the meaning is that he cast that to him and delivered it to him, so it entered his heart.

**(Section)**

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿From among the jinn and mankind﴾.

The exegetes differed over this prepositional phrase: what does it depend on?

Al-Farra' and a group of scholars said: it is an explanation (bayan) of "the people" (al-nas) in whose breasts the whisperer whispers.

The meaning is: he whispers into the breasts of people who are of the jinn and of mankind. That is, the one who whispers into their breasts is of two kinds: humans and jinn. So the whisperer whispers to the jinn just as he whispers to the human.

According to this view, "from among the jinn and mankind" is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause (hal).

This is because it is in the genitive after a definite noun, according to the Basran grammarians. According to the Kufan grammarians, it is in the accusative by "exit from the definite" (al-khuruj min al-ma'rifa). These are their own expressions. Their meaning is that, since it could not serve as an adjective (na't) of a definite noun, it was cut off from it, so its position became the accusative.

The Basrans consider it a circumstantial clause, meaning: "being from the jinn and mankind." This view is very weak, due to the following:

The first: No evidence has been established that a jinn whispers into the breast of a jinn. And it would enter into it just as it enters into a human, and flows within him as it flows within a human. What proof indicates this, such that the verse may be interpreted accordingly?

The second: It is also flawed in terms of wording. For He said: "who whispers into the breasts of mankind." How can "mankind" be explained by "mankind"? The meaning of the statement on their view would be: "he whispers into the breasts of people who are, or being, from the jinn and mankind." Is it permissible to say: "into the breasts of people who are from humankind and others"? This is not permissible, nor is it eloquent in usage.

The third: That He would have divided "mankind" into two parts: jinn and humans. This is not correct, for a thing cannot be the counterpart of itself.

The fourth: The term "jinn" cannot in any way be applied to them as "mankind," neither originally, nor by derivation, nor by usage. Their wording rejects this. The jinn were named "jinn" only from "ijtinan," which means concealment. They are concealed from the eyes of human beings.

They were named "jinn" for this reason, from the expressions "janna al-layl" and "ajannahu" when it covers. And "ajanna al-mayyit" means when he buries the dead in the earth.

He said:

"Do not weep for a dead man after a dead man, whom Ali and Abbas and the family of Abu Bakr buried."

He means the Prophet (ﷺ). From the same root is "al-janin" (the fetus), because it is concealed in its mother's womb. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And when you were fetuses in the wombs of your mothers﴾.

From the same root is "al-mijann" (shield), because the warrior is concealed by it from his enemy's weapon. From the same root is "al-jannah" (garden), because its interior is concealed by trees. From the same root is "al-junnah" (with a damma), which is what protects a person from arrows and weapons. From the same root is "al-majnun" (the insane), because his intellect is concealed.

As for "al-nas" (mankind): there is a connection between it and "al-ins" (humankind) in wording and meaning, and there is a middle derivation between them, namely the arrangement of the permutations of a root with one meaning.

"Al-ins" and "al-insan" are derived from "al-iyناس" (familiarity), which means seeing and perceiving. From this is His saying: ﴿He perceived a fire on the side of the mountain﴾, meaning he saw it. And from it: ﴿If you perceive in them maturity﴾, meaning you perceived it and saw it.

So "insan" (human) was named "insan" because he is sensed (yu’nas), that is, seen by the eye.

As for "al-nas," there are two opinions about it.

One: that it is inverted from "anasa," which is far-fetched, and the original is no inversion.

The second, which is the correct one: that it is from "al-nawas," which is continuous movement.

So mankind was named "nas" for their outward and inward movement, just as a man is named "Harith" and "Hammam," and these are the most truthful of names, as the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The most truthful of names are Harith and Hammam."

Because everyone has an aspiration (hamm) and intention, which is the starting point, and cultivation (harth) and action, which is the end. So every person is a "harith" and a "hammam." Cultivation and aspiration are the movements of the outward and inward, and that is the true meaning of "nawas."

The original of "nas" is "nawas": the waw moved, and before it was a fatha, so it became an alif.

These are the two well-known opinions regarding the derivation of "al-nas."

As for the view of some who say it is from "forgetfulness" (al-nisyan), and that the human was named "insan" because he forgets, and likewise mankind were named "nas" for their forgetfulness: this view is nothing. Where is forgetfulness, whose root is n-s-y, compared to "al-nas," whose root is n-w-s? And likewise, where is it compared to "al-uns" (intimacy), whose root is a-n-s?

As for "insan," it is "fi'lan" from a-n-s. The alif and nun at its end are additional, and nothing other than this is permissible in it at all. For there is no "anasn" in their speech, such that "insan" would be an "if'al" form from it. Nor is it permissible for the alif and nun at its beginning to be additional, for there is no "infa'al" in their speech. So it is specified that it is "fi'lan" from "al-uns."

Since there is no "infa'al" in their speech, it is specified that it is "fi'lan" from "al-uns."

If it were derived from "nasiya," it would be "nisyan," not "insan."

If you say: why not make it "if'lal," whose original is "insiyan," like "layla ihdiyan" (a dark night), and the ya' was dropped for lightness, so it became "insan"?

I say: this is refused by the absence of "if'lal" in their speech, and by dropping the ya' without a cause, and by the claim of something that has no parallel. All of this is invalid. Moreover, it has been said that the original of "al-nas" is "al-unas," so the hamza was dropped, and it became "al-nas."

He cited the verse of the poet:

"Indeed, death-events will come upon the heedless people."

Undoubtedly "unas" is "fu'al." Nothing other than this is permissible in it at all. If the original of "nas" is "unas," then it is the strongest evidence that it is from "uns," and "al-nas" and "al-insan" would be equal in derivation.

The measure (wazn) of "nas" according to this view would be "'al," because its first radical is deleted.

According to the first view, its measure is "fa'l," because it is from "al-nawas."

According to the weak view, its measure is "fal'," because it is from "nasiya." Its final radical was moved to the position of the middle radical, so it became "nas," with the measure "fal'."

The purpose: "al-nas" is a name for the children of Adam. So the jinn do not enter into their designation. Therefore it is not correct that "from among the jinn and mankind" is an explanation of His saying: "in the breasts of mankind." This is clear and there is no obscurity in it.

If it is said: there is no problem in that. For the name "men" (rijal) has been applied to the jinn.

As in His saying: ﴿And that there were men from humankind who sought refuge with men from the jinn﴾.

So when the name "men" has been applied to them, there is nothing preventing the name "mankind" from being applied to them?

I say: this is what deceived the one who said that "nas" is a name for the jinn and humankind in this verse.

The answer to that: the name "men" fell upon them only in a restricted manner, in contrast with the mention of men from humankind. It does not follow from this that the names "nas" and "rijal" apply to them in an unrestricted way.

If you say: "a human of stone" or "a man of wood," and similar things, it does not follow from this that the names "man" and "human" are applied unrestrictedly to stone and wood.

Also, it does not follow from applying the name "man" to a jinn that the name "nas" is applied to him. This is because "nas" and "jinn" are counterparts, and likewise "ins" and "jinn." Allah, glory be to Him, sets the two terms against each other, as in His saying: ﴿O assembly of jinn and humankind﴾, and this is abundant in the Qur'an. Likewise His saying: "from among the jinn and mankind" requires that they are counterparts, so neither enters into the other, unlike "rijal" and "jinn," for they were not used as counterparts. So one does not say "al-jinn wa al-rijal" as one says "al-jinn wa al-ins."

In that case, the verse is a clearer proof against them that the jinn do not enter into the word "nas," because He set "jinn" against "nas." So it is known that neither of the two enters into the other.

The correct view, then, is the second: that His saying "from among the jinn and mankind" is an explanation of the one who whispers, and that they are two kinds: humankind and jinn. So the jinn whispers into the breasts of humankind, and the human likewise whispers into the breasts of humankind.

So the whisperer is of two kinds: humans and jinn. For whispering is the secret casting into the heart. This is common to jinn and humans, although the human's casting and whispering is only through the ear, while the jinn does not need that intermediary, because it enters into the son of Adam and flows within him as blood flows. Moreover, the jinn may appear to someone and whisper to him in his ear like a human does, as in al-Bukhari, from ʿUrwa, from ʿAʾisha, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "Indeed the angels speak in the clouds, and the clouds are the cloud-cover, about a matter that will happen on earth. Then the devils overhear the word and drip it into the ear of the soothsayer, as a flask is filled. Then they add to it a hundred lies of their own."

This is whispering and casting by the devil through the ear.

The analogue of their sharing in this whispering is their sharing in the satanic revelation. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And thus We have made for every prophet an enemy: devils of humankind and jinn, inspiring one another with decorated speech as deception﴾.

So the devil inspires his falsehood to a human, and a human inspires it to a human like himself.

So the devils of humankind and the devils of the jinn share in satanic revelation, and they share in whispering.

According to this, those difficulties and forced interpretations committed by the proponents of the first view are removed. And the verse indicates seeking refuge from the evil of both kinds of devils: the devils of humankind and the devils of the jinn.

According to the first view, the seeking of refuge is only from the evil of the devils of the jinn.

So reflect on it, for it is very marvelous.

This is what Allah has granted of discourse on some of the secrets of these two surahs. To Him belongs praise and favor. Perhaps Allah will assist with an exegesis in this manner, and that is not difficult for Allah. Praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds. We conclude the discussion of the two surahs by mentioning:

**(A Beneficial Principle)**

Concerning what a servant holds fast to against Satan, by which he repels his evil and guards himself from him. These are ten means.

The first: seeking refuge in Allah from Satan. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And if a prompting from Satan afflicts you, seek refuge in Allah. Indeed, He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing﴾.

In another place: ﴿Indeed, He is All-Hearing, All-Knowing﴾. It has already been mentioned that the hearing intended here is the hearing of response, not merely general hearing.

Reflect on the secret of the Qur'an: how it emphasized the description "All-Hearing, All-Knowing" by using the form "huwa," which indicates the emphasis and exclusivity of the attribution, and how it defined the description with "al" in Surah Ha Mim, because the context required this emphasis, and omitted it in Surah al-A'raf, because the context did not need it. For the command to seek refuge in Surah Ha Mim comes after the command to do the most difficult thing to the self, which is repaying the evil of the wrongdoer with good to him. This is something only the patient can achieve, and only one of great fortune attains it, as Allah the Exalted said.

Satan does not let the servant do this. Rather, he shows him that this is humiliation and weakness, and sets his enemy upon him, so he calls him to revenge and adorns it for him. If he fails in that, he calls him to turn away from it, and not to do evil or good to him. So none prefers good to the wrongdoer except one who opposes him and prefers Allah and what is with Him over his immediate portion. So the context was one of emphasis and exhortation. Thus He said in it:

﴿And if a prompting from Satan afflicts you, seek refuge in Allah. Indeed, He is All-Hearing, All-Knowing﴾.

As for Surah al-A'raf: He commanded him to turn away from the ignorant. There is no command in it to repay their evil with good, but only to turn away.

This is easy for souls and not difficult for them to bear.

So Satan's eagerness and effort to prevent this is not like his eagerness to prevent repaying with good. Thus He said:

﴿And if a prompting from Satan afflicts you, seek refuge in Allah. Indeed, He is All-Hearing, All-Knowing﴾.

The difference between these two places has already been mentioned, and between this and His saying in Ha Mim, the Forgiver: ﴿Seek refuge in Allah. Indeed, He is the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing﴾.

In Sahih al-Bukhari, from ʿAdi ibn Thabit, from Sulayman ibn Surad, who said: "I was sitting with the Prophet (ﷺ), and two men were reviling each other. One of them had reddened face and swollen veins. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'Indeed, I know a word which, if he said it, what he feels would go away. If he said: I seek refuge in Allah from Satan the accursed, what he feels would go away.'"

The second safeguard: reciting these two surahs. For they have a wondrous effect in seeking refuge in Allah from its evil, repelling it, and protecting oneself from it. For this reason the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Those who seek refuge have never sought refuge with the like of these two."

It has already been mentioned that he used to seek refuge with them every night at bedtime, and he commanded ʿUqba to recite them after every prayer.

And it has already been mentioned that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever recites them with Surah al-Ikhlas three times in the evening, and three times in the morning, they will suffice him against everything."

The third safeguard: reciting Ayat al-Kursi.

In Sahih al-Bukhari, from the hadith of Muhammad ibn Sirin, from Abu Hurayra, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) entrusted me with guarding the zakat of Ramadan. Then someone came and began to scoop from the food. I seized him and said: 'I will surely take you to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).'" He then mentioned the hadith, until he said: "When you go to your bed, recite Ayat al-Kursi, for there will always be a guardian from Allah over you, and no devil will come near you until morning." The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "He has told you the truth, though he is a liar. That was the devil."

We will mention, if Allah the Exalted wills, the secret behind why this great verse has such great effect in guarding against Satan and the protection of its reciter by it, in a separate discourse on it and on its secrets and treasures, with Allah's help and support.

The fourth safeguard: reciting Surat al-Baqara.

In Sahih, from the hadith of Sahl ibn ʿAbd Allah, from Abu Hurayra, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Do not make your houses graves. Indeed, the house in which Surat al-Baqara is recited, Satan does not enter."

The fifth safeguard: the conclusion of Surat al-Baqara.

It is established in Sahih, from the hadith of Abu Masʿud al-Ansari, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Whoever recites the two verses at the end of Surat al-Baqara in a night, they will suffice him.'" «1»

In al-Tirmidhi, from al-Nuʿman ibn Bashir, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Indeed Allah wrote a book two thousand years before He created creation, from which He sent down two verses with which He concluded Surat al-Baqara. They are not recited in a house for three nights, and Satan comes near it." «2»

The sixth safeguard: the beginning of Surah Ha Mim, the Forgiver, up to His saying: ﴿To Him is the return﴾, along with Ayat al-Kursi.

In al-Tirmidhi, from the hadith of ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Abi Bakr, from Ibn Abi Mulayka, from Zurara ibn Musʿab, from Abu Salama, from Abu Hurayra, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever recites Ha Mim, the Forgiver, up to 'To Him is the return,' and Ayat al-Kursi, in the morning, will be protected by them until evening. And whoever recites them in the evening will be protected by them until morning."

ʿAbd al-Rahman al-Mulaiki, although he was criticized earlier for his memory, the hadith has supporting evidence concerning the recitation of Ayat al-Kursi, and it is acceptable despite its strangeness.

The seventh safeguard:

"There is no god but Allah alone, with no partner. To Him belongs dominion and to Him belongs praise, and He is over all things powerful."

One hundred times.

In the two Sahihs, from the hadith of Sumayy, the freedman of Abu Bakr, from Abu Salih, from Abu Hurayra, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever says: 'There is no god but Allah alone, with no partner. To Him belongs dominion and to Him belongs praise, and He is over all things powerful,' in a day, one hundred times, it will be for him the equivalent of freeing ten slaves, one hundred good deeds will be written for him, and one hundred evil deeds will be erased from him, and it will be a safeguard for him from Satan that day until evening. No one will come with anything better than what he brought, except a man who did more than that."

This is a safeguard of great benefit, of noble advantage, easy and simple for one whom Allah facilitates it for.

The eighth safeguard, and it is among the most beneficial safeguards from Satan: abundant remembrance of Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

In al-Tirmidhi, from the hadith of al-Harith al-Ashʿari, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Indeed Allah commanded Yahya ibn Zakariyya with five words: to act upon them, and to command the Children of Israel to act upon them. He delayed in conveying them. Then ʿIsa said: 'Indeed Allah has commanded you with five words, to act upon them and to command the Children of Israel to act upon them. Either you command them, or I will command them.' Yahya said: 'I fear that if you precede me with them, I will be swallowed up or punished.' So he gathered the people in Jerusalem until it was full, and they sat on the ledges. Then he said: 'Indeed Allah has commanded me with five words to act upon, and I command you to act upon them: the first of them is that you worship Allah and do not associate anything with Him. For the example of one who associates others with Allah is like a man who bought a slave with his pure wealth, with gold or silver, and said: "This is my house, and this is my work, so work and pay me." So he worked and paid to someone other than his master. Which of you would be pleased that his slave should be like that? Indeed Allah has commanded you to pray. When you pray, do not turn about, for Allah directs His face toward the face of His servant during his prayer as long as he does not turn. He has commanded you to fast. For the example of that is like a man in a company with a purse containing musk, so they all admire or are pleased by its scent. Indeed the scent of the fasting person is more pleasant to Allah than the scent of musk. He has commanded you to give charity. For the example of that is like a man whom the enemy captured and bound his hand to his neck, and brought him forward to strike his neck. He said: "I will ransom myself from you with a little or a lot," and he ransomed himself from them. He has commanded you to remember Allah. For the example of that is like a man whom the enemy pursued swiftly on his trail, until he came to a strong fortress and secured himself from them. Likewise the servant does not secure himself from Satan except by the remembrance of Allah." The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "And I command you with five things which Allah commanded me: hearing and obedience, jihad, emigration, and the community. For whoever separates from the community by a span has indeed removed the bond of Islam from his neck, unless he returns. And whoever calls to the call of the Jahiliyya, he is among the embers of Hell."

Then a man said: "O Messenger of God, even if he prays and fasts?" He said: "Even if he prays and fasts. So call them by the name God has given you: the Muslims, the believers, the servants of God."

al-Tirmidhi said: "This is a hadith that is hasan (good), gharib (rare), and sahih (sound)."

al-Bukhari said: "al-Harith al-Ash'ari has companionship (with the Prophet)." He has other narrations besides this one.

In this hadith the Prophet (ﷺ) informed us that a servant can only protect himself from Satan by remembering God. This is exactly what the surah ﴿Say: I seek refuge in the Lord of mankind﴾ indicates, for it describes Satan as "the one who slinks back" (al-Khannas), who, when the servant remembers God, withdraws and shrinks away, and when the servant is heedless of God's remembrance, he seizes the heart and casts into it the whisperings, which are the beginnings of all evil. Thus the servant has protected himself from Satan by nothing like the remembrance of God, the Mighty and Majestic.

The ninth safeguard: wudu' (ablution) and prayer. This is among the greatest means by which one guards against Satan, especially when the powers of anger and desire assail a person, for they are a fire boiling in the heart of the son of Adam.

As in al-Tirmidhi, from the hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "Indeed, anger is a live coal in the heart of the son of Adam. Have you not seen the redness of his eyes and the swelling of his veins? Whoever perceives anything of that, let him lie down on the ground."

And in another report: "Indeed Satan was created from fire, and fire is only extinguished by water."

So the servant extinguishes the live coal of anger and desire by nothing like wudu' and prayer. For it is fire, and wudu' extinguishes it, and prayer, when performed with humility and with turning to God in it, removes the effect of all of that. This is a matter whose experience makes proof of it unnecessary.

The tenth safeguard: restraining excess in looking, speech, food, and mixing with people. For Satan only gains power over the son of Adam and attains his aim through these four doors. Excessive looking leads to admiring, the image of the one looked at falls into the heart, one becomes occupied with it, and thinks about attaining it.

So the beginning of temptation is from excessive looking, as in the Musnad from the Prophet (ﷺ) who said: "A glance is a poisoned arrow of the arrows of Iblis. Whoever lowers his gaze for God's sake, God will bestow upon him a sweetness he will find in his heart until the day he meets Him." Or as he (ﷺ) said.

So great calamities all arise from excessive looking. How many a glance has brought about regrets, not a single regret? As the poet said:

"All calamities have their beginning in the glance,
and most of the fire comes from a little spark despised."

"How many a glance has struck the heart of its owner,
striking like arrows without a bow or string?"

And another said:

"Whenever you sent your gaze out as a scout
for your heart one day, the sights wearied you.
You saw what you are not able to bear entirely,
nor are you patient with part of it."

And al-Mutanabbi said:

"I am the one whose glance brought about his own death:
so who is the seeker, and who is the slain, and who the slayer?"

And from my own verses:

"O you who shoot with the arrows of glances, striving,
you are the one slain by what you shoot, so do not be grieved.

And the one who sends his gaze seeking a cure for himself,
his longing will return to him with tenderness.

You hope for healing through eyeballs in which there is sickness,
have you ever heard of a recovery that came from ruin?

And one who spends his soul pursuing the most ugly of them,
a sincere one stained by the blemish of beauty, which has been plundered.

And one who gives his life in such a thing out of foolishness;
had you known the worth of life, you would not have given it.

And one who sells the good life, which has value,
for a phantom of life, plundered by pains.

You were cheated, by God, a vast cheating;
if you had annulled that contract, you would not have been cheated nor disappointed.

And one who drinks the pure life, all of which is turbid;
before you is the pure rose, not a lie.

And one who gathers firewood in the dark night, standing
for every calamity that draws near to destruction.

Youth passed, and the pursuit of youth, before old age came;
your time was lost between play and sport.

And the sun of your life, its setting has drawn near,
while the dawn in the eastern horizon has not set.

And one who attained union has succeeded, and the darkness of night
and the clouds have cleared from his horizon.

How long will you lag behind while the world has departed,
and the messengers of your Lord have come to you in search?

In the dwelling, now that the camels of the one he loves have journeyed,
there is for the lovesick no residence nor desire.

So lay your cheek on that dust, and say
what the one of longing said in the ages."

"The abode of Mayya, surrounded, circled by Ghaylan,
is not more desirable to him than your ruined abode.

Nor are cheeks, even if they bleed with blood,
more desirable to my eye than your dusty cheek.

Dwellings he loved and was accustomed to,
in the days when attaining union was near at hand.

So whenever those abodes were revealed to him,
he yearns for them as water yearns to flow down a slope.

Longing revives in him the memory of the covenants with them,
so if the heart called him to forgetfulness, it would not respond.

Yet how many a dwelling on earth he is accustomed to,
and for him there is no desire for anything else in time.

In the tents there is no brother of passion who would relieve you,
if you were to confide to him some matter of love, so go abroad.

And in the depths of night, guided
by the fragrance of perfume, not by fire or firewood.

Every cowardly brother returns from a feeble resolve,
and fights the soul, lest it cast you into war.

And take for yourself a light by which you may see,
on the day when the lights are distributed among people by rank.

For the bridge is full of darkness, which none crosses
except with a light that saves the servant in distress."

The point intended: excessive looking is the root of trial.

As for excessive speech, it opens for the servant doors of evil, all of them entrances for Satan. Restraining excessive speech closes off all those doors. How many a war has been started by a single word!

The Prophet (ﷺ) said to Mu'adh: "Do people get thrown on their faces into the Fire except for the harvest of their tongues?"

In al-Tirmidhi: "A man from the Ansar died, and some of the Companions said: 'Paradise be his!' The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'How do you know? Perhaps he spoke about what did not concern him, or was stingy with what would not diminish him.'"

Most sins are generated by excessive speech and looking. These two are the widest entrances of Satan. For the two organs of them never tire or grow weary, unlike the desire of the inner self; for when it is filled, no desire for food remains in it.

As for the eye and the tongue: if left alone, they would not cease from looking and speaking, so their transgression has wide extent, many branches, and great harms.

The early generation (al-salaf) used to warn against excessive looking just as they warned against excessive speech. They used to say: "Nothing needs a long imprisonment more than the tongue."

As for excessive food: it calls to many kinds of evil, for it stirs the limbs toward sins and weighs them down from acts of obedience. Let these two suffice you as evils. How many a sin has been brought about by satiety and excessive food? And how many an act of obedience has it prevented?

Whoever protects himself from the evil of his belly has protected himself from a great evil.

Satan has the greatest control over a person when he fills his belly with food.

For this reason there is a report: "Narrow the channels of Satan by fasting." And the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "No human has filled a vessel worse than the belly."

Even if filling oneself with food had no other harm than that it calls to heedlessness of God's remembrance, and when the heart is heedless of remembrance for a single hour, Satan crouches upon it, promising it, wishing for it, desiring for it, and wandering with it in every valley.

For when the soul is sated, it stirs, wanders, and circles around the doors of desires; and when it is hungry, it calms, humbles, and submits.

As for excessive mixing: it is the incurable disease that brings every evil. How many a blessing has mixing and association taken away! How many enmities has it sown! How many rancors has it planted in the heart, which mountains cannot be removed from, yet in the hearts they do not disappear! So in excessive mixing lies the loss of this world and the next. A servant should only take from mixing in proportion to need.

People are divided into four categories for it. Whenever one category is mixed with another without distinguishing between them, evil enters upon him.

The first: one whose association is like food, which one cannot do without day and night. When one takes his need from him, he leaves the mixing, then when he needs him again, he mixes with him, continually like this. This kind is rarer than red sulfur: they are the scholars of God and His command, the plots of His enemy, the diseases of hearts and their cures, the advisers for God, His Book, His Messenger, and His creatures. In mixing with this kind, the profit is all profit.

The second category: one whose association is like medicine, needed at the time of illness. As long as you are healthy, you have no need of his company. These are those whom one cannot do without for the interest of livelihood, the sustaining of the various kinds of transactions, partnerships, consultation, treatment of illnesses, and the like. When you have fulfilled your need from this kind, their company remains...

The third category: those whose association is like a disease, varying in its degrees, types, strength, and weakness.

Among them is one whose association is like an incurable disease, a chronic sickness, and from him there is no profit in religion or in worldly life. Yet with that, one must lose either religion and the world or one of them.

So whenever the association with this one takes hold and continues, it is a fearful death-illness.

Among them is one whose association is like a toothache whose pain intensifies upon you; when he leaves you, the pain subsides.

Among them is one whose association is like a fever of the spirit. He is the heavy, hateful-minded one, who does not know how to speak so as to benefit you, nor how to listen so as to profit from you, nor does he know himself so as to place himself in his rank. Rather, if he speaks, his speech is like sticks falling upon the hearts of listeners, while he is pleased with his words and delighted by them. He speaks from his mouth whenever he talks, and thinks he is musk by which the gathering is perfumed. And if he is silent, he is heavier than half of a great millstone, which cannot be borne or dragged upon the ground. It is reported of al-Shafi'i (may God have mercy on him) that he said: "No heavy person ever sat beside me without my finding the side he sat on lower than the other side."

I once saw at our shaykh's (may God sanctify his spirit) a man of this kind, and the shaykh was bearing him, though his strength had weakened from bearing him. He turned to me and said: "Sitting with the heavy one is a quartan fever." Then he said: "But our spirits have become addicted to fevers, so it has become a habit for them." Or as he said.

In sum: association with every disagreeable person is a fever of the spirit, whether accidental or constant. It is among the worldly afflictions upon the servant that he is tested with one of this kind, and he has no escape from keeping company with him and mixing with him. So let him treat him with kindness, until God makes for him a way out and an exit from his affair.

The fourth category: one whose association is complete ruin, and whose mixing is like eating poison.

If the one who eats it has an antidote, well; otherwise, may God reward him well with patience. Such people are very numerous among people, may God make few of them. They are the people of innovation and misguidance, who turn others away from the Sunnah of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), who call to its opposite, who bar from the path of God and seek to make it crooked. They make innovation a Sunnah and the Sunnah an innovation, the right wrong and the wrong right.

If you single out monotheism among them, they say: "You disparage the honor of the saints and the righteous."

If you single out following the Messenger of God (ﷺ), they say: "You have dismissed the imams who are followed."

If you describe God with what He described Himself with, and with what His Messenger described Him with, without exaggeration or diminution, they say: "You are one of the anthropomorphists (mushabbiha)."

If you command what God and His Messenger commanded of the good and forbid what God and His Messenger forbade of the evil, they say: "You are one of the troublemakers."

If you follow the Sunnah and abandon what opposes it, they say: "You are one of the misguiding people of innovation."

If you devote yourself to God, the Exalted, and leave them to the carrion of the world, they say: "You are one of the deceivers."

If you abandon what you are upon and follow their desires, you are with God among the losers, and with them among the hypocrites.

So the sound judgment, entirely, is to seek the pleasure of God and His Messenger even by angering them, and not to busy yourself with appeasing them, nor with asking them to be appeased, and not to mind their blame or their hatred. For this is the very essence of your perfection, as one said:

"And if the blame of a deficient one reaches me,
it is my testimony that I am excellent."

And another said:

"Indeed, it has increased my love for myself that I
am hated by every man who is of no worth."

So whoever wakes the doorkeeper and guardian of his heart from these four entrances, which are the root of the trials of the world, namely excessive looking, speech, food, and mixing,

and uses the nine means mentioned above that protect him from Satan,

has taken his share of success, closed the doors of Hell upon himself, opened upon himself the doors of mercy, and his outward and inward have been immersed in it, and he will soon praise, at death, the outcome of this remedy.

At death people praise piety, and in the morning people praise the night journey. And God is the Granter of success; there is no lord but Him, and no god besides Him.

[Chapter on his guidance (ﷺ) in visiting the sick]

He (ﷺ) used to visit those of his Companions who fell ill, and he visited a boy who used to serve him, from the People of the Book, and he visited his uncle, who was a polytheist, and he offered them both Islam; the Jew accepted Islam, but his uncle did not accept it.

He used to draw near to the sick person, sit at his head, and ask him about his condition, saying: "How do you find yourself?"

It is mentioned that he used to ask the sick person what he desired, saying: "Do you desire anything?" If he desired something and it was known that it would not harm him, he would order it for him.

He used to pass his right hand over the sick person and say: "O Lord of mankind, remove the affliction, and heal him, for You are the Healer; there is no healing except Your healing, a healing that leaves no sickness behind."

He used to say: "Wipe away the affliction, Lord of mankind; in Your hand is the healing, and none can remove it except You."

He used to supplicate for the sick three times, as he said to Sa'd: "O God, heal Sa'd, O God, heal Sa'd, O God, heal Sa'd."

Whenever he entered upon a sick person he would say to him: "No harm; it is a purification, God willing."

Sometimes he would say: "An expiation and a purification."

He used to perform ruqyah (incantation) for one who had a sore, a wound, or an ailment: he would place his index finger on the ground, then raise it and say: "In the name of God. The dust of our land, with the spittle of some of us, our sick is healed by the permission of our Lord." This is in the two Sahihs, and it nullifies the wording that came in the hadith of the seventy thousand who enter Paradise without reckoning, and that they do not perform ruqyah nor seek ruqyah. His saying in the hadith "they do not perform ruqyah" is an error by the narrator; I heard Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah say that.

He said: "The hadith is only: 'They are those who do not seek ruqyah.'"

I say: That is because these people entered Paradise without reckoning, for the perfection of their monotheism. For this reason He negated from them seeking ruqyah, which is asking people to perform it upon them. For this reason He said: "and upon their Lord they rely," so for the perfection of their reliance upon their Lord, their tranquility toward Him, their trust in Him, their contentment with Him, and their placing their needs with Him, they ask people for nothing, neither ruqyah nor anything else, and no omen arises for them that would turn them from what they intend, for omens diminish monotheism and weaken it.

He said: "The one who performs ruqyah is giving charity and doing good, and the one who seeks ruqyah is asking. The Prophet (ﷺ) performed ruqyah and did not seek it, and he said:

'Whoever among you is able to benefit his brother, let him benefit him.'"

If it is said: "What do you say about the hadith in the two Sahihs from A'isha (may God be pleased with her), that the Messenger of God (ﷺ)

'whenever he went to his bed, would join his palms, then blow into them and recite: "Say: He is God, One" and "Say: I seek refuge in the Lord of the daybreak" and "Say: I seek refuge in the Lord of mankind," and he would wipe with them whatever he could of his body, beginning with them over his head and face and what faced forward of his body, doing that three times.' A'isha said: 'When the Messenger of God (ﷺ) fell ill, he would order me to do that for him.'"

The answer: this hadith has been narrated with three wordings. The first is this one.

The second: that he used to blow upon himself.

The third: she said, "I used to blow over him with them (the chapters), and wipe with his own hand for its blessing." In a fourth wording: "Whenever he fell ill, he would recite over himself the Mu'awwidhat and blow." These wordings explain one another.

The Prophet (ﷺ) would blow over himself, but his weakness and pain prevented him from passing his hand over his whole body. So he would order 'Aisha to pass his hand over his body after he had blown himself. This is not at all a case of seeking cure by incantation (istirqa'), and she did not say, "He would order me to perform ruqya on him." Rather, she mentioned wiping with his hand after blowing over his body. Then she said, "He would order me to do that to him," meaning: that I should wipe his body with his hand as he himself used to do.
